Phase 05 · 9–12 hours

Components & function.

A handle is not decoration added to a cup. A lid, foot, spout, and body form one system of forces, clearances, movement, and use.

Map an interfaceBuild the pouring vessel

Aim

Design relationships, then test use.

Prerequisite

Secure joins, moisture matching, controlled profiles, and basic shrinkage awareness.

By the end

You can prototype interfaces, fit a lid, balance a handle, tune a spout, and evaluate comfort, stability, pouring, and cleaning.

Deliverables

Paper mockups, handle trials, a lid-fit matrix, a pour-system study, and one 0.6–1 L pouring vessel.

05.1

Function lives at the interface.

What changes when a beautiful object must be lifted, tilted, cleaned, and returned to a table?

Hand ↔ handle

Comfort + leverage

Clearance, section, attachment points, and center of mass determine grip and wrist load.

Lid ↔ gallery

Fit + movement

Clearance must accommodate clay shrinkage, glaze thickness, firing movement, and removal.

Foot ↔ table

Stability + lift

Contact area, flatness, weight distribution, and edge finish govern wobble and handling.

Lab · Full-scale paper and clay mockups90 min
  1. Choose a cup or small vessel. Trace its profile full-size.
  2. Prototype three handles in stiff paper: close-to-body, high-loop, and side-loop. Tape each to the drawing.
  3. Mock them in clay and attach to a sacrificial body at compatible moisture.
  4. Grip with one, two, and three fingers. Simulate full weight with water in a separate safe container, not unfired clay.
  5. Score comfort, clearance, leverage, visual integration, and cleanability.
Functional testing happens twice.Prototype geometry before firing. Before any drink or food test, use a studio-approved, manufacturer-designated food-contact glaze on its recommended clay and firing. Keep experimental surfaces away from food-contact areas. Reject body cracks, shivering or flaking, sharp edges, crawling, unstable texture, and other uncleanable or unstable defects; treat crazing conservatively. “Lead-free,” “non-toxic,” gloss, and home vinegar or lemon screens are not certification. Unknown, altered, layered, or sale-bound systems need qualified guidance and, where appropriate, laboratory leach testing. Microwave, dishwasher, oven, freezer, and flame suitability are separate claims requiring evidence.
05.2

Fit is a range, not a single line.

Lab · Lid-fit matrix2 hours

Make six small jars and three lid systems: drop-in flange, cap, and inset. For each, make a close and generous clearance.

  1. Label body and lid as a pair; dry together but prevent sticking.
  2. At leather hard, test lift, slide, rotation, and finger access.
  3. After firing, compare fit changes. Record clay, forming state, dimensions, glaze placement, firing, and result.

No universal clearance guarantees fit. Your matrix creates evidence for your exact clay–glaze–forming–firing system. Follow the studio’s lid-firing method; unless a tested method specifies otherwise, keep ordinary glaze off mating surfaces, allow for glaze run and kiln movement, and never force a stuck fired lid. Test expendable matched samples before the final vessel.

Foot check

05.3

A pour is a coordinated system.

Flow path

Reservoir → inlet → spout → lip

The inlet admits liquid, the spout accelerates and guides it, the lip separates the stream. Handle position controls the tilt through that whole path.

Air must replace liquid

Glugging often signals restricted air entry or competing flow. Lid fit, venting, fill level, inlet size, and tilt angle interact; change one variable at a time.

Lab · Pour-system test2–3 hours
  1. Build three small test bodies with different spout inlet areas or lip cuts.
  2. When safe to wet-test, use the same water volume, target vessel, and pour angle sequence.
  3. Video from the side. Record start lag, stream coherence, glugging, drips, lid movement, wrist angle, and residual liquid.
  4. Revise the weakest interface rather than remaking every part.
05.4

Project: one complete pouring vessel.

Integrated project

0.6–1 L, built for an actual ritual.

Name the drink, user, serving context, target capacity, and cleaning method. Combine at least two handbuilding methods and include body, handle, lid or open fill point, spout, and stable foot.

  1. Make two full-scale paper profiles and a handle mockup. Mark center of mass at empty and estimated full states.
  2. Build components at compatible moisture states. Support attachments while they equalize.
  3. Document clearances and critical dimensions before drying.
  4. After the appropriate firing and studio approval, test capacity, lift, pour at three fill levels, drip, lid retention, stability, and cleaning access.
  5. Write one redesign priority based on observed use—not taste alone.

Inspiration · look comparatively

Function can carry ceremony, story, and character.

Ask what each component does mechanically—and what it changes visually or socially.

Knowledge check · 3 questions

Pause. Predict. Diagnose.

Choose one answer for each situation. Open a hint when needed; explanations appear after you check all three.
